answer:
The boundary can return **timed-out after the transport has completed at logical time 99**. Whether that is a reliability defect depends on a rule the supplied contract leaves open.

If the harness completes the transport at 99 and advances the clock to 100 in the same JavaScript turn, `FakeTransport` releases its slot and resolves its promise immediately. The boundary’s success handler cannot run until the turn yields, so the synchronous deadline callback records `timed-out` first. The later success handler cannot change that result. If the harness instead awaits the response before advancing, the boundary records `ok` and cancels the timer. See [transport.mjs](/var/folders/kb/clk179sd5qq5htsth48gfk5c0000gn/T/brooks-runtime-study-eadyFr/repo/shared/transport.mjs:24) and [request-boundary.mjs](/var/folders/kb/clk179sd5qq5htsth48gfk5c0000gn/T/brooks-runtime-study-eadyFr/repo/shared/request-boundary.mjs:27).

That behavior conflicts with a contract in which transport settlement before 100 determines success. It is consistent with one in which the boundary must process the promise before the deadline. The supplied context specifies neither interpretation, nor the rule for completion exactly at 100 ([context.md](/var/folders/kb/clk179sd5qq5htsth48gfk5c0000gn/T/brooks-runtime-study-eadyFr/repo/RT-40/context.md:3)).

The cancellation protections are supported by the visible path: the service passes the boundary signal to the transport, and deadline or parent cancellation aborts pending transport work. The transport then releases its slot and abort listener. On processed success, it has already released those resources, and the boundary cancels its timer and removes the parent listener. The boundary also observes a later rejection from abandoned work. In the 99-to-100 case, the transport slot is already released; the observed issue is the response outcome, not a demonstrated slot leak.

No conclusion about production timing or traffic impact follows from this synthetic example.
